items.title: Electricity generated by source in a European country, 2022
points: The bar chart shows how much electricity a European country generated from six sources in 2022, measured in terawatt hours.
Gas was by far the largest source at 112 TWh, while hydroelectric power was the smallest at only 18 TWh.
Gas produced almost three times as much electricity as coal, which stood at 38 TWh.
Interestingly, wind generated 71 TWh, slightly more than nuclear power at 64 TWh, while solar contributed 29 TWh.
Overall, the country relied heavily on gas, although wind had already become the second most important source.

items.title: Students completing their degree within four years by faculty at a university, 2015 and 2025
points: The chart compares the percentage of students who completed their degree within four years in six faculties of a university in 2015 and 2025.
Medicine had the highest completion rate in both years, rising from 83% to 88%, whereas engineering had the lowest, at 49% in 2015.
Engineering also showed the biggest improvement, climbing by 12 percentage points to 61% in 2025.
Law was the only faculty where the rate fell, dropping slightly from 71% to 69%.
Overall, completion rates improved in five of the six faculties over the decade.

items.title: Average one-way commuting time by mode of transport in one city, 2023
points: The bar chart illustrates the average one-way commuting time for six modes of transport in one city in 2023.
Bus commuters had the longest journeys, at 47 minutes, while people who walked had the shortest, at just 18 minutes.
A bus journey therefore took more than two and a half times as long as a walk to work.
Surprisingly, driving took 32 minutes on average, which was quicker than both the train at 41 minutes and the tram at 36 minutes.
Overall, the active modes, cycling at 22 minutes and walking, were the fastest ways to commute, most likely because they are used for shorter trips.

items.title: Adults meeting physical activity guidelines by age group in one country, 2005, 2015 and 2025
points: The chart shows the percentage of adults in five age groups who met physical activity guidelines in 2005, 2015 and 2025.
The highest figure was 55% for 18 to 29 year olds in 2015, while the lowest was 14% for people aged 75 and over in 2005.
Older groups improved the most, with the 60 to 74 age group rising from 28% to 42% and the over-75s almost doubling from 14% to 26%.
In contrast, the youngest group was slightly less active in 2025 than in 2005, at 51% compared with 52%.
Overall, activity still declines with age, but the gap between the youngest and oldest groups narrowed from 38 to 25 percentage points.

items.title: Unemployment rate by highest qualification for men and women in a European country, 2024
points: The bar chart compares unemployment rates for men and women with five levels of qualification in a European country in 2024.
The highest rate was 16.8% for women with no diploma, and the lowest was 3.1% for men with a postgraduate degree.
Unemployment fell steadily as qualifications rose; for men it dropped from 14.2% to 3.1%, meaning the least qualified were more than four times as likely to be unemployed.
Women had higher rates at every level except vocational qualifications, where their rate of 5.2% was below the male figure of 6.1%.
Overall, education made a far bigger difference to unemployment than gender did.

items.title: Overseas visitors to five regions of a country, 2023
points: The chart shows the number of overseas visitors to five regions of a country in 2023, in millions.
The Central region was the most popular destination with 12.4 million visitors, while the East attracted the fewest, only 3.1 million.
This means the Central region received four times as many visitors as the East.
The South came second with 9.8 million, followed by the West with 6.5 million and the North with 4.2 million.
Overall, of the 36 million visits, about a third went to the Central region, so tourism was heavily concentrated in one area.

items.title: Wheat yield in five countries, 2000 and 2020
points: The bar chart compares wheat yields in tonnes per hectare in five countries in 2000 and 2020.
Country E had the highest yield in both years, reaching 7.3 tonnes in 2020, while Country C had the lowest, at 2.1 tonnes in 2000.
Country C made the most remarkable progress, more than doubling its yield to 4.3 tonnes, and Country A also rose sharply from 3.2 to 4.6 tonnes.
By contrast, Country D was the only country where yields fell, slipping from 4.4 to 4.2 tonnes.
Overall, yields improved in four of the five countries, and the gap between the most and least productive narrowed considerably.

items.title: Average weekly use of five devices by age group in one country, 2024
points: The chart shows how many hours per week three age groups spent using five types of device in 2024.
The highest figure was 28 hours of smartphone use among 16 to 24 year olds, while the lowest was just 1 hour on games consoles for people aged 45 to 64.
Smartphone use fell with age, from 28 hours for the youngest group to 11 hours for the oldest.
Television showed the opposite pattern, with the oldest group watching 17 hours, almost three times the 6 hours of the youngest.
Overall, younger people preferred personal devices, while older people remained loyal to television.

items.title: Proportion of household waste recycled in seven districts of one city, 2024
points: The bar chart illustrates the percentage of household waste that was recycled in seven districts of one city in 2024.
District 3 had the highest recycling rate at 61%, whereas District 4 had the lowest at only 27%.
The best district therefore recycled more than twice the proportion of the worst.
Only two districts recycled more than half of their waste, District 3 and District 5 at 52%, while the rest ranged from 27% to 46%.
Overall, performance varied widely across the city, with an average of about 43%.

items.title: Research funding by field at a university, 2014 and 2024
points: The chart compares research funding across six academic fields at a university in 2014 and 2024, in millions of US dollars.
Medicine received the most funding in both years, rising from 42 to 58 million dollars, while the humanities received the least, falling from 6 to 4 million.
The most striking change was in computing, where funding tripled from 12 to 36 million, almost catching up with engineering at 38 million.
Physics was the other field to lose money, dropping from 18 to 15 million.
Overall, total funding grew from 122 to 161 million dollars, but the increase went mainly to medicine and computing.
